title: No faith speaks with one voice
description: Every tradition is a loose family of subtraditions: Christian worship in a Baptist chapel and an Orthodox church can look very different.

facts.text: Smart wrote that every religious tradition shows itself as a loosely held-together family of subtraditions.

title: What 'unaffiliated' means
description: The unaffiliated are people who call themselves atheist, agnostic or 'nothing in particular'; some still hold beliefs or keep practices.

facts.text: Pew's religiously unaffiliated are people who describe themselves as atheist, agnostic or 'nothing in particular', and some of them hold religious or spiritual beliefs and practices.

title: America's separation of church and state
description: The First Amendment bars an established religion and protects free exercise; the Census Bureau cited church-state separation in 1976.

facts.text: The First Amendment says: "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof."
In 1976 the Census Bureau's director said a religion question on the mandatory census would appear to infringe upon the traditional separation of church and state.

title: France's laïcité
description: France's 1905 law guarantees freedom of conscience and recognizes, pays for and subsidizes no religion; religion is private and public schools stay free of conspicuous religious symbols.

facts.text: France's 1905 law says the Republic ensures freedom of conscience, and neither recognizes, pays for nor subsidizes any religion.
French laïcité treats religion as a private matter and keeps a secular public sphere.
A French law of 15 March 2004 bans public school students from wearing conspicuous religious symbols, such as Muslim headscarves, Sikh turbans, Jewish skullcaps and large crosses.

title: India's secularism
description: India's constitution protects religious freedom; 'secular' joined its preamble in 1976; its secularism balances equal respect for all religions with neutrality and allows religious personal law.

facts.text: India's constitution protected religious freedom and banned religious discrimination from the start; the word secular was added to its preamble in 1976.
Britannica describes Indian secularism as balancing Gandhi's sarva dharma sama bhava, the equality of all religions, with Nehru's neutrality toward religion.
In India, Muslims may follow Islamic law and Hindus Hindu law in family matters such as marriage and inheritance.

title: Atheism and its long history
description: Atheism denies belief in God or spiritual beings; India's ancient Lokayata school already rejected god, soul and afterlife.

facts.text: Britannica defines atheism as the critique and denial of metaphysical beliefs in God or spiritual beings; the word comes from the Greek atheos, "godless".
India's Lokayata school, also called Carvaka, rejected god, an immaterial soul and the afterlife, and accepted perception alone as a reliable source of knowledge.
No doctrinal works of the Lokayata school survive; only fragments remain.

title: Agnosticism
description: Huxley coined 'agnostic' in 1869; agnostics leave the question of God open rather than denying it.

facts.text: T. H. Huxley introduced the word agnosticism in 1869 at a meeting of the Metaphysical Society in London.
Huxley said the word came to him as the opposite of the "Gnostic" of Church history, who professed to know so much about things of which Huxley was ignorant.
Atheism denies that God exists, while agnosticism leaves the question open, finding it unanswered or unanswerable.

title: Secular humanism
description: Humanism is a nonreligious ethical life stance; many humanists are atheists or agnostics; Holyoake coined 'secularism' in 1851.

facts.text: Humanists International describes humanism as a democratic and ethical life stance affirming that human beings have the right and responsibility to give meaning and shape to their own lives.
Humanists International says many humanists are atheists and others agnostic, and that humanists do not believe in gods or an afterlife.
George Holyoake first used the word secularism in 1851, for a nonreligious civic and ethical philosophy.

title: The rise of American nones
description: The unaffiliated share of US adults grew from 16% (2007) to 29% (2023-24) and has recently plateaued.

facts.text: In Pew's Religious Landscape Studies, religiously unaffiliated Americans rose from 16% of adults in 2007 to 23% in 2014 and 29% in 2023-24.
The 2023-24 Religious Landscape Study surveyed 36,908 US adults.
Pew reports that the share of religiously unaffiliated Americans has plateaued in recent years after a long period of growth.
In the 2023-24 study, 19% of US adults were raised Christian and now say they are religiously unaffiliated.

title: Who the nones are
description: Most US nones say 'nothing in particular'; atheists and agnostics are minorities among them.

facts.text: In Pew's 2023 data, 17% of US religious nones identified as atheist, 20% as agnostic and 63% as "nothing in particular".

title: Believing without belonging
description: Most US nones believe in God or a higher power; many are spiritual; their reasons focus on questioning teachings and disliking institutions.

facts.text: Pew found that most US religious nones believe in God or some other higher power.
About half of US nones say spirituality is very important in their lives or think of themselves as spiritual.
Two-thirds of US nones say they question a lot of religious teachings or don't believe in God, and 47% cite disliking religious organizations as a very important reason.

title: The secularization thesis
description: Berger (1967) defined secularization and, like many sociologists, expected modernization to erode religion; Bruce still defends the thesis, and structural secularization happened in much of Europe.

facts.text: In The Sacred Canopy (1967), Peter Berger defined secularization as "the process by which sectors of society and culture are removed from the domination of religious institutions and symbols", as when education left church authority.
The early Berger saw secularization as an inevitable result of modernization and, like many sociologists of his time, saw little future for religion.
Sociologist Steve Bruce defended the secularization thesis in a 2011 book, tying religion's decline to modernization.
Most sociologists of religion agree that institutions separating from religion has happened in much of Europe, at least.

title: Berger's about-face
description: In 1999 Berger declared the world 'as furiously religious as it ever was', calling the secularized-world assumption false.

facts.text: In 1999 Berger wrote that "the assumption that we live in a secularized world is false" and that the world is "as furiously religious as it ever was".

title: Why the world's religious map changes
description: From 2010 to 2020 switching grew the unaffiliated, while youthful, higher-fertility religious populations grew fastest; religious numbers still rose.

facts.text: From 2010 to 2020 the Muslim share of the world rose 1.8 points to 25.6%, the Christian share fell 1.8 points to 28.8%, and the unaffiliated share rose nearly a point to 24.2%.
Religious switching, especially people raised Christian shedding their religious identity, explains much of the unaffiliated population's growth from 2010 to 2020.
Muslims grew fastest from 2010 to 2020, helped by their youthfulness, while the unaffiliated are older and have lower fertility than Christians, Muslims and Hindus.
From 2010 to 2020 the number of Muslims grew by 347 million and the number of Christians by 122 million.

title: Juergensmeyer's cosmic war
description: Juergensmeyer studies religious motives in violence: 'cosmic war' frames a conflict as good against evil, though he holds that violence has social, political and economic causes.

facts.text: Mark Juergensmeyer's Terror in the Mind of God draws on interviews to study violence among Christian, Muslim, Jewish, Hindu, Sikh and Buddhist groups.
Juergensmeyer uses "cosmic war" for the image of a broader conflict between good and evil, right and wrong, not just a fight fought for religious reasons.

Juergensmeyer says he does not believe religion causes violence, which happens for a complex variety of social, political and economic reasons; religion brings "a structure of justification and meaning".

title: Cavanaugh's myth of religious violence
description: Cavanaugh argues there is no timeless essence of religion, so 'religious violence' is a misleading category shaped by power.

facts.text: In The Myth of Religious Violence (2009), William Cavanaugh argues there is no transhistorical and transcultural essence of religion; what counts as religious or secular depends on configurations of power.
Cavanaugh argues that the idea of religion as non-rational and prone to violence is one of the foundational legitimating myths of Western society.

title: Mystics across traditions
description: Sufis, Kabbalists, Christian contemplatives like Teresa of Ávila and Zen practitioners each seek the sacred directly.

facts.text: Britannica defines Sufism as mystical Islamic belief and practice in which Muslims seek the truth of divine love and knowledge through direct personal experience of God.
Kabbalah is esoteric Jewish mysticism; its great book, the Zohar ("Book of Splendour"), appeared in medieval Spain and in some circles gained a sanctity rivaling the Torah's.
The Spanish Carmelite nun Teresa of Ávila described the soul's progress toward God through prayer in The Interior Castle.
Zen, a school of East Asian Buddhism named from the Sanskrit dhyana, "meditation", seeks awakening through meditation as "a special transmission outside the scriptures".

title: William James's marks of mysticism
description: James (1902) named ineffability, noetic quality, transiency and passivity; the first two are enough to call a state mystical.

facts.text: In The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902), William James named four marks of mystical states: ineffability, noetic quality, transiency and passivity.
James held that ineffability and a noetic quality are enough to call a state mystical: it defies expression in words, yet feels like a state of knowledge.

title: One path or many?
description: Perennialists see a common core in mystical experience; constructivists like Katz argue each tradition shapes the experience itself.

facts.text: James saw in Hinduism, Sufism and Christian mysticism one tradition "hardly altered by differences of clime or creed", but admitted that on a wider view "the supposed unanimity largely disappears".
Perennialists such as Aldous Huxley (1945) hold that mystical doctrines transcend all cultures and religions.
In 1978 Steven Katz argued that there are no pure, unmediated experiences: a mystic's religious setting shapes, even over-determines, the experience itself.

title: 'New religious movement', not 'cult'
description: Every religion was new once; 'cult' went from a neutral term to a slur, so scholars prefer 'new religious movement' to avoid prejudging a group.

facts.text: Eileen Barker notes that all religions were new at their inception; early Christianity was a sect within the Judaic tradition, and early Methodism a sect within Christianity.

Church, sect, denomination and cult were once technical, non-judgmental terms in sociology; in popular speech today "cult" can suggest a dangerous pseudo-religion that exploits recruits with brainwashing.
Britannica calls "new religious movement" the generally accepted term for what is sometimes called, often pejoratively, a cult.
Barker argues that to discover whether a movement commits crimes or abuse, it must be defined independently of those traits; since the 1970s scholars have preferred "new religious movement".
Britannica notes that the concept of brainwashing peaked in the 1970s but has since lost credibility.

title: Judging any group by its actions
description: New movements differ widely, so each must be judged by what it believes and does at a given time and place.

facts.text: Barker writes that new religious movements differ in beliefs, practices, leadership, finances and potential for harm, and that no activity is typical of them and atypical of older religions.

Because new religious movements differ so much, Barker says each must be looked at according to what it believes and does at a particular time and place, without confusing the movement, its leaders and its members.
In 1988 Barker founded Inform, an educational charity giving information about minority religions that is as accurate and up to date as possible.

title: The 1893 Parliament of Religions
description: Chicago's 1893 Parliament began the modern interfaith movement, though Christians dominated and Native Americans were excluded.

facts.text: The World's Parliament of Religions met in Chicago from 11 to 27 September 1893, in the building that became the Art Institute of Chicago.
The 1893 Parliament is regarded as the origin of the modern interfaith movement.
English-speaking Christians delivered 152 of the 194 papers at the 1893 Parliament, and Native Americans were excluded.
In his final address at the 1893 Parliament, the Hindu monk Vivekananda said every religion's banner would soon read "Help and not fight".

title: Nostra Aetate
description: The Catholic Church's 1965 declaration rejects nothing true and holy in other religions, esteems Muslims, decries antisemitism and urges dialogue.

facts.text: Nostra Aetate, proclaimed by Pope Paul VI on 28 October 1965, says the Catholic Church "rejects nothing that is true and holy" in other religions.
Nostra Aetate says the Church regards Muslims with esteem and decries hatred and displays of antisemitism directed against Jews.
The same declaration says the Church "ever must proclaim Christ", while urging dialogue and collaboration with followers of other religions.

title: Ground rules for dialogue
description: Swidler's Dialogue Decalogue: dialogue aims to learn; each partner describes their own faith; compare ideals with ideals and practice with practice.

facts.text: Leonard Swidler's Dialogue Decalogue holds that the essential purpose of dialogue is to learn.
Swidler's rules say each participant describes their own faith, and that ideals should be compared with ideals and practice with practice.

title: Where believers actually live
description: Most Muslims live in the Asia-Pacific region, and more Christians live in sub-Saharan Africa than in Europe.

facts.text: In 2020, about 59% of the world's Muslims lived in the Asia-Pacific region.
In 2020, 30.7% of the world's Christians lived in sub-Saharan Africa, compared with 22.3% in Europe.

title: 'Allah' as the Arabic word for God
description: Allah is the standard Arabic word for God, used by Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews as well as Muslims.

facts.text: Allah is the standard Arabic word for God and is used by Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews as well as by Muslims.
The name Allah is probably a contraction of the Arabic al-Ilah, "the God".
